case_studies.title: ROCm InferaSim: Cut LLM Serving Trial Costs and Deploy the Best Configuration
case_studies.abstract: Serving an LLM efficiently depends on the engine, how the model is split across GPUs, precision, scheduler settings, speculative decoding, KV-cache management, and prefill-decode disaggregation. The best configuration depends on the model, hardware, workload, and objective. Operators usually find it by trial and error. Exhaustively measuring the candidates in our study would take about 25,000 GPU-hours. ROCm InferaSim predicts serving performance from a few short measurements. Choices such as batch size, prompt length, and GPU count change the amount of work per GPU without changing the kernels. ROCm InferaSim benchmarks each distinct set of kernels once, on at most one node. We call this measurement an anchor. Analytical laws carry that anchor to other deployments that run the same kernels. For multi-node deployments, ROCm InferaSim reduces the configuration to a single-node equivalent, measures it, and scales the result analytically. A simulator replays multi-turn traffic, and a tuning agent searches configurations using the predictions. On AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs with vLLM, SGLang, and ATOM, 11 anchors took 9.1 GPU-hours, against 204 GPU-hours to measure the 226 fixed-length configurations they cover. On 172 configurations, time per output token has 8.1% median error. On a multi-turn coding workload, throughput is within 8%. For 159 disaggregated deployments, none used as an anchor, throughput is within 5.5%. A five-candidate short list contains a deployment within 12% of the best feasible pairing of model and latency target.
case_studies.summary: ROCm InferaSim helps cloud engineers predict LLM serving performance with far fewer GPU hours by measuring key kernel configurations once and extrapolating to other setups. It builds a lightweight simulation and tuning agent that reduces the search for optimal batch size, GPU count, and other settings from thousands of trials to just a handful of short runs, achieving within‑10% accuracy. The result is a 90% reduction in trial time while maintaining near‑optimal throughput for large‑language‑model deployments.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AMD Instinct GPUs for LLM serving, run a few short anchor tests (≈10 GPU‑hours) with your chosen engine and model, then use InferaSim to predict best batch size and GPU count; adjust your deployment settings accordingly and validate with a quick benchmark.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical tool for LLM deployment optimisation that directly benefits IT engineers working with cloud and GPU infrastructure, offering measurable performance gains. While the abstract suggests a working system, it does not detail open-source availability or production deployment, hence a moderate maturity score. The methodology is actionable and could be monetised by service or tooling within 90 days. Overall impact and potential are high.

case_studies.title: RuntimeTickets: Source-Grounded Security Obligations for Agent Skills
case_studies.abstract: Third-party Agent Skills extend what an autonomous agent can do, but a malicious Skill can hide data exposure or output manipulation inside a legitimate workflow. Neither reading a Skill's description nor granting it tool permissions tells whether its execution meets the user's security requirements. We introduce RuntimeTickets, a protocol that enforces and audits these requirements while a Skill runs. From released malicious-Skill datasets we derive a risk model and build adversarial-benign Skill pairs. From the task's delivery contract, a language model proposes security obligations for that task. Each obligation cites the Skill lines it answers, and the ticket tightens the host's approvals into fine-grained allowed actions but never loosens them. A runtime gate checks the recipient, object and amount of every outbound send before forwarding it, and trusted monitors record the effects within their observation scope. The ticket links these checks and observations to the approved obligations of each Skill run, and a deterministic decoder turns the ticket's status into governable data flows and verifies each obligation. Neither enforcement nor decoding involves a language model, so text injected by a Skill can change the proposal but never the rule that decides a send. We evaluate RuntimeTickets at the network egress boundary of three unmodified agent frameworks against production Skill scanners and runtime baselines, among them an AgentBound-derived allow-list and SkillGuard. RuntimeTickets eliminated both failure modes of current Skill defenses, overlook (malicious Skills let through) and overkill (benign Skills blocked): its overlook rate was 0.0% and its overkill rate 0.0%, while the scanners erred on both sides. RuntimeTickets ties approved requirements to verifiable execution evidence and offers a common foundation for the safe and auditable deployment of third-party Skills.
case_studies.summary: RuntimeTickets lets you enforce and audit security rules for third‑party agent skills while they run, linking each skill’s actions to a set of fine‑grained obligations. They built a protocol that checks every outbound send and records evidence, achieving zero overlooked or over‑blocked attacks in tests. This means you can safely run external skills without trusting the skill itself.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure with autonomous agents, add RuntimeTickets: step 1: define security obligations for each skill task, step 2: deploy the runtime gate to check outbound traffic against those obligations, step 3: use the ticket decoder to audit and enforce compliance. If your org uses third‑party skills, check that your egress filters support fine‑grained per‑skill rules immediately.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a protocol for enforcing security obligations in third‑party agent skills, directly relevant to IT infrastructure security and compliance. The approach is evaluated on real agent frameworks and shows zero failure rates, indicating a mature, deployable solution. It offers a clear, actionable tool that IT engineers could adopt or commercialize within 90 days, such as integrating RuntimeTickets into existing cloud or SaaS environments.

case_studies.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
case_studies.abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.
case_studies.summary: This research shows that by rewriting a language model’s earlier reasoning into a compact state before new tool results, the model can produce shorter, cheaper future reasoning without retraining. The authors tested this on open‑weight models and found that compact histories typically cut token use and cost, while still keeping task quality. For cloud infra managers, this could lower the compute cost of running large‑language‑model agents that generate long reasoning traces.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑based agents, you can reduce run costs by implementing a compaction step: 1) capture the model’s reasoning history before any tool output, 2) rewrite that history into a concise state record, 3) feed the compact history back to the model for the next step. Check that your agent framework supports injecting state; if not, adapt the compaction as an external pre‑processing step.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a method to reduce reasoning token usage by compacting prior reasoning traces, which can lower operational costs for cloud-based LLM services and improve efficiency in agentic deployments. The approach is experimentally validated on open-weight models, but no publicly released code or production-ready system is provided, indicating moderate maturity. The findings are actionable for IT engineers looking to reduce cloud spend on LLM APIs, making the monetisation potential moderate. Overall, it has a moderate real-world impact, moderate maturity, and moderate monetisation potential, yielding a total score of 40.

case_studies.title: False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts
case_studies.abstract: An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.
case_studies.summary: This study shows that LLMs can give users a false sense of safety when they cannot see official weather alerts. The researchers built a test set of 117 real U.S. National Weather Service alerts, ran them through different LLM pipelines, and found that a production setup that feeds the model alerts produced 0% false reassurance, while blind prompts led to high false reassurance rates. The work highlights the risk of deploying LLMs that lack up‑to‑date alert data and provides a dataset and code for testing your own systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage an LLM‑powered support chat, here is what to do: 1) Ensure your model receives real‑time weather alerts as input; 2) Verify the pipeline with a test set like the one released; 3) Disable blind or neutral prompts that could trigger false reassurance. This flags a risk: if your org uses LLMs for customer queries about weather, check that the model can access live alerts before deployment.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on a very narrow domain (weather alerts) and evaluates a specialized LLM pipeline. While it does provide released data and code, the practical impact on IT infrastructure, software engineering, or automation is minimal. The technology is not broadly applicable to the target audience, and there is little evidence of immediate commercial or operational use. Consequently, all criteria score low and the total remains below 30.

case_studies.title: Correctness Firewalls for Synthesized Database Components
case_studies.abstract: For the first time in history, high-performance code is cheap. Today's coding agents can generate bespoke, instance-optimized data systems with excellent performance, and such agents will continue to improve as LLMs advance. But a purely agentic approach, even when validated with strong testing techniques, does not automatically inherit the correctness guarantees our community has spent decades building. We propose a middle ground between hand-crafted and agent-crafted systems: correctness firewalls, lightweight design patterns under which a synthesized component can affect a system's performance but never its results. Behind a correctness firewall, agents are free to synthesize fast components while the overall system remains correct. We present three case studies, each demonstrating a different type of firewall: cardinality estimation (advisory), searching sorted data (guarded), and data compression (certified). In early experiments, synthesized components search sorted data up to 3x faster than human-designed learned indexes and can compress text 1.5x smaller than Zstd. Drawing on these case studies, we outline a research agenda for how data management systems can exploit coding agents without giving up their hard-won correctness guarantees, from protecting synthesized code to measuring the cost of correctness.
case_studies.summary: This paper tackles the risk of using AI‑generated database code by introducing "correctness firewalls"—lightweight design patterns that let synthetic components boost performance without compromising data integrity. The authors built three types of firewalls (advisory, guarded, certified) and showed that AI‑synthesised sorted‑search code ran up to 3× faster than hand‑crafted learned indexes, while AI‑compressed text was 1.5× smaller than Zstd. These results suggest that cloud teams can safely adopt AI‑generated database components by wrapping them in appropriate firewalls.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud databases, you can adopt these firewalls: step 1 – identify the component type (search, compression, estimation); step 2 – apply the corresponding firewall pattern (advisory, guarded, certified); step 3 – validate outputs against a gold standard before deployment.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a novel framework for ensuring correctness of agent-generated database components, which could influence future DB tooling. However, it remains largely conceptual with limited empirical validation, no released code or proven production deployment, and no clear immediate commercial use case for IT engineers in the next 90 days.
